meaning.evidence: Every instruction survives: "Mobiles and cordless phones are fine", "don't go lying on the garage floor", "wait 30 minutes after the last lightning or thunder", "People who've been struck don't carry an electrical charge, so they're safe to touch." "Way too many people muck about for far too long" tilts waiting into fooling around, a small shift.

sense.evidence: "power point", "Mobiles", "cops a lightning strike", "on the cards", "quick smart" all fit. "muck about" implies messing around rather than simply delaying.

authenticity.evidence: Natural Australian phrasing: "close enough for the storm to have a crack at you", "it starts bucketing down", "through piss-poor planning", "all this dodgy behaviour".

register.evidence: A thorough retelling in Aussie idiom with swearing inside the dial ("bloody useless", "piss-poor planning", "a hell of a lot"), but in standard spelling and close to the original's structure; a strong level 4 more than a full pub yarn. Headings stay as is: "Minimizing the Risk".

tone.evidence: The warning stays a warning, but "Others, through piss-poor planning, get stuck outside" adds a scolding edge the neutral safety text doesn't have.

flow.evidence: Reads as if written that way: "the lightning threat ramps up as a storm comes in, peaks when it's right overhead, then slowly drops off as it moves away."

variety.evidence: Good spread, with "when there's storms about" recurring ("when there's thunderstorms about", "when there's storms about" three more times) and "carry on" twice.

essence.evidence: Still the NWS safety page: the slogan "When Thunder Roars, Go Indoors!", the behaviour-determines-risk point, the 30-minute rule.

problems.quote: Way too many people muck about for far too long
problems.original: Too many people wait far too long
problems.why: "muck about" means fooling around, not just delaying.

problems.quote: Others, through piss-poor planning, get stuck outside
problems.original: Others, due to poor planning, are caught outside
problems.why: Allowed by the dial, but adds a scolding note to neutral safety advice.
Heading left with US spelling while the body is Australian.

A.summary: Natural, vivid and faithful; a solid level-4 retelling with a slightly scolding swear.

meaning.evidence: Effectively the original sentence for sentence ("Substantial buildings and hard-topped vehicles are safe options."), so nothing is lost; the original's slip "what can do to lower their risk" is carried over as "lightning'n what can do to lower their risk".

sense.evidence: The few swaps fit: "power point", "Mobiles and cordless phones are safe", "every bloke'n sheila".

authenticity.evidence: Eye-dialect sprinkled on formal prose: "'ave a lightning safety plan, and cancel or postpone activities early", "Monitor weather conditions and get to a safe place before the weather becomes threatenin'." No Australian would say it like this.

register.evidence: Largely untranslated; Aussie is limited to "ya", "yer", dropped g's and "every bloke'n sheila". Far lighter than level 5.

tone.evidence: The serious, instructional tone is untouched: "Call 911 and monitor the victim."

flow.evidence: Clunky joins: "windows'n don't lie on a garage floor", "struck by lightning'n what can do", and inconsistent "lightnin'" against "lightning" in the same sentence.

variety.evidence: Relies on the same few devices: g-dropping and "yer" ("yer personal risk", "yer behaviour", "yer personal risk").

essence.evidence: The original's content is all there, but the stray contractions flatten it into neither the plain guide nor a retelling: "Lightnin' victims don't carry an electrical charge".

problems.quote: 'ave a lightning safety plan, and cancel or postpone activities early
problems.original: Have a lightning safety plan, and cancel or postpone activities early
problems.why: Eye-dialect on untranslated formal prose; pastiche.

problems.quote: struck by lightning'n what can do to lower their risk
problems.original: struck by lightning and what can do to lower their risk
problems.why: Garbled join, and the original's missing subject carried over.

problems.quote: There's no safe place outside when thunderstorms are in the area.
problems.original: There is no safe place outside when thunderstorms are in the area.
problems.why: Text left largely untranslated against a level-5 brief.

B.summary: Essentially the original with dropped g's and a few swaps; safe on meaning, far short of the brief.

meaning.evidence: All points kept, including "Mobiles and cordless phones are right", "don't go lyin' on a garage floor", "wait 30 minutes", "A lightnin' victim doesn't carry an electrical charge, so they're safe to touch."

sense.evidence: "pull the pin on things" for cancelling, "give ya a squiz" for insight, "quick smart", "cops a lightnin' strike" all fit exactly.

authenticity.evidence: Sounds like a local: "Best way to look after yerself with lightnin'? Don't be anywhere near it.", "Gettin' Yer Head Round the Threat".

register.evidence: Full drawl and idiom throughout, with no swearing (allowed, not required), but it stays a tidy retelling of the guide rather than a full yarn with asides.

tone.evidence: Warning kept firm and plain: "If the sky's lookin' nasty or ya hear thunder, get inside somewhere safe straight away."

flow.evidence: Smooth and natural aloud: "don't touch anythin' plugged into a power point, don't touch the plumbin', and don't touch a phone with a cord on it."

variety.evidence: Varied, with some recurrence of "leave it way too late" (twice) and "carry on" (three times).

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the safety guide, slogan and all: "When Thunder Roars, Go Indoors!"

problems.quote: heaps leave it way too late to get somewhere safe
problems.original: many people wait far too long to get to a safe place
problems.why: "leave it way too late" repeats from the opening paragraph.

C.summary: Clean, natural, faithful retelling; a little restrained for level 5.

meaning.evidence: All points survive with colour hung off them: "Not in the backyard, not out in the paddock, nowhere.", "pull the pin on the footy or the barbie or whatever it is", "Straight away, not after one more over." "Don't stand there." adds an imperative that elaborates calling for help.

sense.evidence: "the whole box and dice" for all the habits, "one more over" for delaying, "Good on 'em" for those who go inside early: each fits.

authenticity.evidence: Real Aussie talk: "Some head inside at the first sign of a storm. Good on 'em.", "Most people do make it inside, fair enough, but then some go and put themselves at risk anyway".

register.evidence: A full retelling in a speaker's voice with asides and direct address ("Listen,", "Here's the thing.", "But here's the kicker"), swearing light and within the dial ("the bloody thing"). Level 5 weight.

tone.evidence: The urgency is, if anything, sharpened: "Now, once yer inside, it's not over.", "Now, this bit's important: a lightnin' victim doesn't carry an electrical charge".

flow.evidence: Short punchy fragments read well aloud ("Thirty minutes."), though "A rain shelter, a little shed, an open vehicle? No good. Not safe, any of 'em." is a bit choppy.

variety.evidence: Wide spread of idiom and openers: "Listen,", "Here's the thing.", "Take the first graph.", "the whole box and dice", "one more over".

essence.evidence: Every section and the slogan are kept; it reads as the same guide told by a person: "So remember, it's how you carry on when thunderstorms are about".

problems.why: Added instruction; elaborates the call to action but is not in the original.

problems.quote: No good. Not safe, any of 'em.
problems.original: Rain shelters, small sheds, and open vehicles are not safe.
problems.why: Slight stacking of the same point.

D.summary: The best yarn: full level-5 voice with apt local colour, and the safety message kept urgent and complete.

meaning.evidence: All points survive: "Mobiles and cordless phones are right", "wait 30 minutes", "Lightnin' victims don't carry an electrical charge and are safe to touch."

sense.evidence: "pull the pin on things", "a bit of a squiz", "quick smart" fit; nothing takes a wrong sense.

authenticity.evidence: Mostly natural, but "'Ave a lightnin' safety plan" is stage eye-dialect, and "get inside a safe spot straight away" is an odd frame.

register.evidence: Consistent drawl and idiom, but stays close to the original's sentence shapes ("While some people head inside at the first sign of a thunderstorm, heaps leave it way too late"); level 4 rather than 5.

tone.evidence: The warning stays plain and serious: "Call 911 and keep an eye on the victim."

flow.evidence: Readable, with clunky spots: "get inside a safe spot straight away", "keep off phones with a cord, electrical gear, the plumbin', and windows and doors".

variety.evidence: "safe spot" is leaned on heavily ("no safe spot outside", "get to a safe spot", "can't get to a safe spot", "get inside a safe spot"), and "Last of all" appears twice.

essence.evidence: Recognisably the guide in every section, slogan kept.

problems.quote: get inside a safe spot straight away
problems.original: get inside a safe place immediately
problems.why: "safe spot" is repeated throughout, and "inside a spot" is awkward.
"Last of all" repeats from the earlier paragraph.

E.summary: Faithful and natural enough, a level-4 retelling that leans hard on "safe spot".
